opus-5.5.text:
Training is the easy case. You have a huge batch of tokens and you process all of them in parallel, so you're doing a lot of arithmetic for every byte you pull from memory. The chips are happy because they're compute-bound, and that's what they're built for.

Inference, especially autoregressive decoding, flips that. You generate one token at a time, and each step depends on the one before. So for every new token you have to stream all the model's parameters through the chip, plus the attention keys and values for the whole context so far, and you do only a tiny bit of math on each one. You end up memory-bandwidth-bound. The expensive multiply units are mostly sitting idle waiting for data.

You can batch many users together, and that amortizes the cost of loading the weights. But the key-value cache is per-sequence, so it doesn't amortize. As contexts get longer and you serve more people, that cache becomes the dominant cost, both in memory capacity and in bandwidth. That's why a lot of my work has been about shrinking it. Multi-query attention, where all the heads share a single set of keys and values, came out of exactly this problem. Since then people have explored grouped-query attention, local attention mixed with global layers, quantizing the cache, and sharing it across layers.

Then there's latency. In training nobody cares how long a single example takes, only total throughput. For a product, a person is waiting for the next word. So you're trading off batch size against responsiveness, and you're splitting the model across chips in ways that add communication overhead.

So the challenge is mostly about memory: making the model and its state cheap to move around, rather than making the math faster. If you co-design the architecture with the serving system, you can get very large improvements in cost, often bigger than you'd get from new hardware. And cost matters a lot, because if you want billions of people talking to these models every day, inference cost decides whether the product is viable.

r001.rationale: It contrasts training, which processes many tokens in parallel, with autoregressive inference, which generates one token at a time and depends on the previous token.

r002.rationale: It says each generated token requires streaming the attention keys and values for the context so far, making inference memory-bandwidth-bound.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that training is a throughput problem and inference is a memory bandwidth and latency problem, and those want very different machines.

When you train, you process enormous batches. Every weight you load from memory gets used across thousands of tokens at once, so the arithmetic intensity is high and the accelerator is actually doing math most of the time. That is what GPUs and TPUs are built for. You can also afford to spend a long time on it, because nobody is waiting on the other end of a request.

Inference flips that. For generation, you produce one token at a time, and to produce that token you have to read every parameter of the model out of memory. If you are serving a single user, you load hundreds of gigabytes of weights to do a trivial amount of arithmetic per byte. The chip sits idle waiting on memory. So the whole game becomes how many sequences you can pack into a step so that each weight read gets amortized across many users.

Then the key value cache makes it worse. Attention means each step also has to read back the state for every prior token in every sequence in the batch. That memory grows with batch size and with context length, so the thing you want more of, bigger batches, is exactly the thing that eats your memory. That is actually what pushed me toward multi query attention. Sharing keys and values across heads shrinks that cache by a large factor and that directly translates into higher batch sizes and cheaper decoding.

The other half is latency. Training can tolerate pipeline bubbles and slow interconnect because you only care about total throughput. In inference a person is reading as you generate, so you care about time per token, and that means you are often splitting a single model across many chips just to get the bandwidth, which puts you at the mercy of the interconnect for every step.

So if I had to summarize it, training hardware wants flops, and inference hardware wants bandwidth, memory capacity, and fast chip to chip communication. The industry built for the first, and most of the clever work on the inference side is about reshaping the model and the serving system so they look more like the first problem than they naturally do.

r001.rationale: It contrasts training on enormous batches with inference generating one token at a time, communicating that inference has less parallelism.

r002.rationale: It says each inference step reads the key-value cache state for every prior token, and describes inference as memory-bandwidth limited.

astra-6.text:
Training is a relatively straightforward infrastructure problem in the sense that you’ve got this enormous batch of work, and you can optimize for throughput. With inference, you have a user waiting for an answer, so latency matters a lot. And you’re generating one token at a time, so you can’t parallelize across the output sequence the way you can during training.

If you’re serving one request, you end up reading a huge number of model weights to do relatively little computation. So you’re often limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. You want to batch requests together to reuse those weights, but you can’t wait forever to assemble a batch. And the requests have different lengths, they arrive at different times, and their attention caches consume memory as they grow.

So the challenge is keeping the hardware busy while still giving each user a fast response. That makes inference a much more dynamic scheduling and memory-management problem than training.

r001.rationale: It says inference generates one token at a time and cannot parallelize across the output sequence as training can.

r002.rationale: It identifies model-weight reads as a memory-bandwidth bottleneck and mentions growing attention caches, but does not state that accessing attention keys and values for every generated token causes the bottleneck in naive inference.

sol-6.1.text:
Training is a relatively predictable workload. You have these big batches, and you’re doing large matrix multiplications, which is what the hardware is good at. Inference is trickier because you’re generating one token at a time, and you want to get that token back to the user quickly. If your batch is small, you can spend much more time moving the model’s weights out of memory than actually doing arithmetic.

So there’s a tension between throughput and latency. You’d like to batch a lot of requests together to use the hardware efficiently, but you don’t want everybody waiting around. And the requests are all different lengths, with different amounts of cached attention state. The infrastructure challenge is keeping the hardware busy while managing all that memory and still making the system feel fast.

r001.rationale: It contrasts training’s large batches with inference generating one token at a time, communicating that inference has less parallelism.

r002.rationale: It mentions moving model weights from memory and cached attention state, but does not identify accessing attention keys and values for every generated token as the bottleneck.
